title: Two ways (Didache 1)
hook: there are two ways, one of life and one of death, and great is the difference
tomorrow: how does a hillside of scattered wheat become one loaf?

segments.voice: The letters went to Rome and Corinth first, and the address kept widening: read as if to you. That block is closed. A new one opens, with the teachers who came after, in their own words.
screen: `READ AS IF TO YOU.` → `THE TEACHERS WHO CAME AFTER.`

segments.voice: A maps app offers two routes: the fast one, and the one without tolls. Most days hold forks like that, so small nobody notices choosing. A short old book opens right at one. There are two ways, it says, one of life and one of death, and great is the difference between them. No greeting. No author's name. Just the fork, in the first line. The book is the Didache, a Greek word for teaching. Tradition calls it the Teaching of the Twelve Apostles.
screen: `TWO ROUTES ON THE MAP.` → `ONE OF LIFE, ONE OF DEATH.` → `THE DIDACHE: TEACHING.`

segments.voice: So what does the way of life ask? The Didache starts where Jesus starts. First, love the God who made you. Second, your neighbor as yourself. Then a line with a twist: whatever you wouldn't want done to you, don't do to another. Jesus says it as a do: "all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets." The Didache gives it as a line you won't cross. The fork itself is older still. Moses sets it before Israel: "I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life." And that golden line has a famous Jewish cousin. The Talmud tells of a man who asks the sage Hillel to teach him the whole Torah while standing on one foot. Hillel answers: what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor. That's the whole Torah; the rest is commentary. Go and learn. Here's what's shared: the same don't, and the same sense that one plain line can hold a whole way of living. And the honest difference: for Hillel the line sums up the Torah, and the next step is to go and study it. The Didache sets it inside the way Jesus taught, with love of God first, and leads on to baptism and a shared meal. One line, two homes.
screen: `LOVE GOD, THEN NEIGHBOR.` · `WHAT YOU WOULDN'T WANT, DON'T DO.` · `HILLEL ON ONE FOOT.` · `SHARED LINE, TWO HOMES.` · then, large: `THE WAY OF LIFE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one fork waiting for you today: a reply, a bit of money, a word about someone who isn't there. Name which way is life, name what usually pulls you the other way, and settle now what you'll do when that pull shows up.
Two ways. The Didache's opening: a way of life and a way of death, and a great difference between them.
Pocket this one: the way of life, which begins with loving God and the neighbor beside you. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: The Didache isn't read in most Sunday services, but Christians study it as an early handbook, and its two ways and golden rule echo teaching that churches give new believers.

chat.meaning: The Didache gives the golden rule as a 'don't', as Hillel does in the Talmud. Shared ground, honestly different homes: the Torah's summary, and the way Jesus taught.

notes: Written 2026-10-13 in the year-2-4 recipe; rewritten 2026-10-15 in recipe v3 (wisdom shape: what does the way of life ask?). Title, word, carry and sources kept; Psalm 1 and Matthew 5:44 dropped from the voice for length; the Hillel story added.

Unity thread (owner, 'more alike than we think'): Hillel and the man who asked to learn the whole Torah on one foot (Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a), paraphrased: 'what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor; that is the whole Torah, the rest is commentary; go and learn.' Shared: the 'don't' form of the golden rule and the sense that one line holds a whole way of life. Honest difference: for Hillel it summarizes the Torah and sends the asker to study; the Didache sets it inside the way Jesus taught, after love of God, leading to baptism and the meal (Didache 7, 9). Neither is ranked. Confirm with a Christian Keeper and, ideally, a Jewish reader.
